evaluation.positioning_hook: After his wife, children, and sister are destroyed by a predatory crime family, a devout father spirals into vigilante justice and a Catholic reckoning that could save him or finish him.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The revenge engine is immediate and legible, and the Catholic-grief angle gives it a distinct emotional lane. But the script’s extreme violence and heavy theological dialogue narrow the audience to adult crime-drama buyers rather than broad commercial four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early: a bereaved brother/father is pulled into a war with the Risaldi family, and the story keeps returning to that central collision. The opening is more elliptical than clean, but once the family massacre and Jacob’s vigilante path lock in, the hook is easy to explain.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and even Victor all have strong moral contradictions that create playable tension, especially in the confession scenes and the final ballroom confrontation. The downside is that several supporting players are defined more by function than by inner life, so the character engine is strong but not uniformly deep.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s Catholic framework is not decorative; confession, adoration, penance, and grace are built into the dramatic spine. That gives the material a more specific identity than a standard mob-revenge piece, even if the underlying revenge architecture is familiar.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story escalates cleanly through the massacre, the alleyway killing, the docks raid, and the Christmas showdown, with strong forward pressure once Jacob and Jodie converge on Victor. Some midsection scenes lean on repeated moral debate, but the plot keeps moving toward a clear endgame.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of Catholic ritual, family trauma, and organized crime gives the script a fresh surface and a memorable emotional frame. Still, the core engine is a familiar revenge/crime structure, so the originality comes more from texture than from a wholly new dramatic premise.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Risaldi family hierarchy, the police response, the church spaces, and the civic fallout create a world with real social pressure and recurring institutions. The mansion, club, docks, and church all feel story-generating, though the world is still centered on a few key nodes rather than a fully sprawling ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very distinct register: operatic violence filtered through Catholic guilt, family ritual, and public prayer. The contrast between confession-booth intimacy and brutal mob spectacle gives it a hard-to-mistake tonal identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real seeds of deeper material here: Victor’s ideology, Ethan’s moral fracture, Jodie’s grief-as-function, and Jacob’s relationship to sin all suggest more beneath the plot. The script sometimes states its themes directly, but the underlying emotional architecture is strong enough to imply more depth than the surface action.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jacob/Jodie, Ethan/Victor, Ethan/Frankie, and Jacob/Father Michael all generate distinct dramatic energy, and the family structure gives the story recurring relational pressure. It’s not an ensemble in the broad sense, but the key pairings are strong enough to keep the movie alive scene to scene.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, white, Catholic, working-class father and brother, grief-stricken widower.
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is the emotional center of the film: a devout, soft-spoken family man whose faith becomes both refuge and indictment after his wife and children are murdered. He starts as a man trying to survive grief through prayer and therapy, then hardens into a vigilante who believes justice is the only way to keep his family from disappearing twice.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea or Joel Edgerton in The Gift — a contained, inward performance that has to hold rage, shame, tenderness, and moral collapse in the same frame. It gives an actor a full grief-to-violence arc with confession scenes, breakdown scenes, and a final reckoning that can reset how audiences see them.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, white, police officer, Catholic, Jacob’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is the procedural and emotional counterweight to Jacob: a cop who treats work like survival and grief like something she can outrun. She’s tough, defensive, and deeply wounded, and the script gives her a strong arc from professional control to personal collapse and finally to the choice to protect what remains of her family.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Amy Adams in Sharp Objects or Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk a chance to play authority, fragility, and buried pain without softening the edges. It’s a prestige supporting part with real close-up emotional payoff and a final-act moral authority beat.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, white, morally conflicted member of the Risaldi family.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the family’s conscience, or at least the closest thing it has to one: principled, frightened, and constantly trying to step out of the machine without fully knowing how. He’s the most human Risaldi on the page, which makes him the script’s bridge between the family’s brutality and the possibility of redemption.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted, spiritually torn role that gave Paul Dano in Prisoners or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog so much traction — a character who can be read as weak until the performance reveals the steel underneath. It offers an actor a major moral-pressure role with long scenes of argument, confession, and uneasy alliance.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 60s, white, patriarch, organized-crime boss, father.
lead_characters.hook: Victor is the film’s true antagonist and ideological engine: composed, cruel, and terrifyingly self-justifying. He doesn’t just command violence; he frames it as order, purity, and necessity, which makes him more dangerous than a standard crime boss and gives the movie its coldest scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire the chance to make authority feel intimate and monstrous at once. It’s a commanding villain part with monologues, psychological domination, and a final-act collapse that would attract a serious character actor.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, white, violent enforcer, son of Victor.
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s most volatile weapon: theatrical, sadistic, and desperate for approval he can never actually earn. He’s terrifying because he performs cruelty like a language, but the script also lets him crack under Victor’s gaze, which makes him more than a simple brute.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, high-wire role that gave Jack O’Connell in Starred Up or Ben Foster in Hell or High Water a chance to go fully combustible. It’s a juicy villain turn with physical menace, emotional instability, and a brutal final confrontation.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, white, enforcer, son of Victor.
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the quieter brother who still lives inside the same violent system, which makes him tragic rather than merely threatening. He’s loyal, frightened, and increasingly aware that obedience has become its own kind of death sentence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that gave Michael C. Hall in Safe or Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire a chance to play menace with vulnerability underneath it. It’s a strong supporting part for an actor who can make fear, loyalty, and self-betrayal all register at once.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, white, physically imposing enforcer.
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt instrument: huge, brutal, and mostly defined by action rather than speech. He’s less psychologically elaborate than Martin or Ethan, but he functions as a terrifying embodiment of the family’s violence and obedience.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of physically dominant role that gave Tom Hardy in Bronson or Liev Schreiber in Ray Donovan a chance to weaponize presence before dialogue. It’s a strong showcase for an actor with imposing physicality and controlled menace.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the film’s spiritual ballast and one of its best tonal devices: warm, funny, pastoral, and quietly serious about sin and grace. He gives the movie a moral vocabulary that never feels abstract because he speaks like someone who actually lives inside the community’s pain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Mark Rylance in The Outfit or Brendan Gleeson in Calvary a chance to turn wisdom into dramatic tension. It’s a prestige supporting part with sermon scenes, private counsel, and the ability to anchor the film’s faith dimension without becoming a symbol.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, white, Victor’s wife, former stripper, mother.
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is trapped inside the family’s hierarchy but still carries enough interior life to make her more than a victim or accessory. The script positions her as someone who has adapted to abuse without ever fully consenting to it, which makes her final scenes especially painful.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Laura Linney in Ozark a chance to play contained devastation under pressure. It’s a sharp supporting part with emotional humiliation, fear, and a late-stage tragic turn.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the family’s last remaining innocence, and the script uses him as a living moral question rather than a plot device. He’s quiet, observant, and vulnerable, which makes every scene around him feel like a test of whether anyone in this world can still choose mercy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that gave Noah Jupe in Honey Boy or Jacob Tremblay in Room a chance to carry emotional weight without overplaying it. It’s a sensitive, high-impact part that can become the audience’s moral anchor.

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical storytelling with limited needs for fire/smoke, burning-photo imagery, and crowd/atmospheric enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Multiple gunshots, blood effects, body impacts, a hammer killing, fire/smoke effects, and practical wound work.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming or theatrical specialty crime drama
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a prestige crime-thriller with awards-adjacent faith-and-grief framing or a streamer original.

budget.note: Contemporary production keeps the spend contained, but the church, mansion, club, docks, police, and crowd-heavy finale all need careful scheduling, plus practical blood/fire work and multiple night exteriors.

casting.note: Jacob, Jodie, Victor, Ethan, and Martin all need actors who can carry long moral confrontations, while Marcus adds a child-performance requirement that matters emotionally in the final act.

development.note: The script’s strongest identity comes from its Catholic framework and grief language, but the middle section leans heavily on dialogue-driven moral debate, so the buyer will weigh tone consistency and pacing discipline.

comp_set.title: A History of Violence
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns family identity and buried violence into a contained crime drama where the home front is as dangerous as the criminal world.

comp_set.title: Sicario
comp_set.why_it_comps: It shares the grim law-enforcement pressure, moral corrosion, and escalation from investigation to violent reckoning.

comp_set.title: Calvary
comp_set.why_it_comps: The Catholic setting, confession-driven moral inquiry, and dark spiritual register make it a close tonal neighbor.

comp_set.title: Prisoners
comp_set.why_it_comps: The grief-fueled descent into vigilantism and the pressure of missing children give it a similar emotional engine.

comp_set.title: Wind River
comp_set.why_it_comps: It matches the bleak crime-thriller lane where trauma, justice, and revenge are braided into a prestige genre package.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who buy prestige crime thrillers with moral weight, especially viewers drawn to Catholic imagery, family tragedy, and revenge stories with a conscience.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64, slightly male-skewing but viable with adult women who respond to grief-driven drama and faith-based moral conflict; educated, streamer-friendly, prestige-drama audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, limited VFX, and a mostly dialogue-and-performance-driven structure keep it in indie feature territory, though the finale needs practical effects and controlled crowd work.

lane_fit.lane: prestige crime thriller with faith-based emotional spine
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where crime, grief, and moral reckoning are the product, not just the backdrop. The Catholic confession material and family trauma give it a distinct hook for buyers looking for elevated genre with awards-adjacent seriousness.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the story resolves the Risaldi conflict and does not present a clean sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.what_it_means: The confession, adoration, and penance framework gives the movie a clear thematic identity that can separate it from standard revenge-crime fare. That makes it attractive to buyers who want prestige genre with a spiritual spine and to actors who want material with moral consequence.
strengths.evidence: The confession booth scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and Jacob’s Act of Contrition structure the emotional arc rather than sitting on top of it.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jacob is a serious actor role
strengths.what_it_means: The lead has a full grief-to-violence transformation, which is exactly the kind of part that can attract a name actor looking for a prestige turn. That gives the package a real anchor point for financing and festival positioning.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s therapy blowup, the alleyway killing, the confession, and the final confrontation with Victor all demand different registers from the same performer.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family villainy is highly playable
strengths.what_it_means: Victor, Martin, Ethan, and Frankie each occupy a different moral position inside the same criminal system, which creates multiple casting hooks and strong scene-to-scene tension. That helps the project sell as more than a one-man revenge story.
strengths.evidence: Victor’s domination scenes, Martin’s sadism, Ethan’s conscience, and Frankie’s collapse all generate distinct dramatic textures.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world is specific without being expensive
strengths.what_it_means: Churches, a mansion, a club, docks, police interiors, and a few key exteriors create a rich crime world without requiring tentpole scale. That makes the script easier to finance than a broader mob epic while still feeling lived-in.
strengths.evidence: The story repeatedly returns to the adoration chapel, Risaldi mansion, docks, and club as its core arenas.

strengths.what_it_means: The final confrontation resolves the revenge engine while also landing on grief, forgiveness, and survival, which broadens the movie’s aftertaste beyond simple catharsis. That gives the film a better chance at word-of-mouth among adult audiences who want more than a body count.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s breakdown when Katherine appears, Jodie’s embrace, Ethan taking Marcus, and the final church/recovery montage all land the emotional landing gear.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige crime thriller with a built-in spiritual differentiator: a grief-fueled revenge story told through Catholic ritual, family collapse, and confession. It has the kind of actor-facing lead role and contained contemporary production footprint that can get a serious buyer to lean in without needing tentpole scale.

items.area: The opening massacre is structurally overloaded.
items.detail: The first 15 pages stack the family introduction, the Risaldi intrusion, the murder of Jay, and the burn-photo reveal in a way that front-loads a lot of information before the audience has fully oriented to the central relationships. It’s powerful material, but it asks the buyer to trust a very dense opening before the movie has settled its emotional center.

items.area: The middle leans hard on moral dialogue.
items.detail: Several key stretches, especially the confession scenes and the Jodie/Jacob arguments, are built around characters explaining their worldview rather than forcing the plot forward through action. That gives the film its voice, but it also creates a pacing conversation for buyers who want the thriller engine to stay taut.

items.area: The violence is extreme and buyer-sensitive.
items.detail: Jay’s murder, the child endangerment, the hammer killing, and the repeated execution-style deaths push the material into very dark territory. That is fine for mature streaming or specialty theatrical, but it narrows the buyer pool and will be a content conversation in any mainstream room.

The script names multiple songs and artists, including Come Back by The Five Stairsteps, O Holy Night, Petals by Hole, Good Looking by Suki Waterhouse, 500 Miles by Peter, Paul and Mary, Clair de Lune, L’Amour Toujours, I Want More, and 311. That is a real sync-clearance and budget conversation if the music is meant to stay on the page as written.

items.area: Marcus is emotionally important but lightly dramatized.
items.detail: The child role matters a great deal to the ending and to Victor’s ideology, but he has relatively little active scene time compared with the adults. That makes him more of a symbolic pressure point than a fully developed engine, which is fine for the story but worth noting in casting and audience expectation conversations.

issues.headline: The main friction is concentration: the script is strongest when it’s in confession, confrontation, and family reckoning, but it spends a lot of time explaining its moral universe before the final collision. The other real buyer conversation is content and clearance — this is a very dark movie with a long named-music list and several scenes that will immediately define its rating lane.
